subtopic_detail: choosing antiresorptive therapy after a vertebral fracture when the estimated glomerular filtration rate sits below the bisphosphonate cut-off
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 78-year-old woman in the fracture liaison clinic. She tripped on a rug three weeks ago, landed on her buttocks, and has had band-like mid-back pain since. Imaging of the thoracolumbar spine shows a wedge deformity at T12 with loss of about a third of the anterior vertebral height, and no other fracture.

She takes perindopril and a thiazide for blood pressure and has never taken a bone-specific medication. She has been on colecalciferol for six months and drinks two glasses of milk daily. Her bloods today show a corrected calcium of 2.32 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), phosphate 1.1 mmol/L (0.8-1.5), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (>50), creatinine 152 micromol/L (45-90) and an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 28 mL/min/1.73m2, unchanged across three readings over the past two years. Parathyroid hormone and serum protein electrophoresis are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Focal tenderness over the T12 spinous process, no neurological deficit in either leg
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L (2.15-2.60), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (>50), eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73m2, parathyroid hormone within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Thoracolumbar radiographs: T12 wedge deformity with about one third anterior height loss, no other vertebral fracture

lead_in: Which pharmacological therapy would you start for her bone health?

options.text: Six monthly subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: Denosumab is cleared by the reticuloendothelial system rather than the kidney, so it needs no dose adjustment at this level of renal function and is the preferred antiresorptive when bisphosphonates are excluded. Her vitamin D is replete and her corrected calcium is mid-range, which is the prerequisite before the first injection because hypocalcaemia risk rises steeply in advanced renal impairment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and Metabolism)

options.text: Annual intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: Zoledronic acid carries a higher renal threshold than the oral bisphosphonates and is contraindicated below 35 mL/min/1.73m2, so her filtration rate excludes it more firmly than it excludes alendronate. The near pair here is the assumption that switching a bisphosphonate from oral to intravenous solves a renal problem, when in fact it worsens it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Bisphosphonates)

options.text: Daily subcutaneous teriparatide 20 micrograms with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: Teriparatide is an anabolic agent reserved under Australian subsidy for very severe osteoporosis, typically two or more fractures with a low bone density result, and it has not yet been shown to be needed here after a single vertebral fracture. It would also require an antiresorptive afterwards to hold the gain, which returns you to the same decision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and Metabolism)

options.text: Continued calcium and vitamin D alone with a repeat bone density scan in two years
options.rationale: A minimal trauma vertebral fracture in this age group establishes osteoporosis irrespective of the bone density result, so waiting for a scan delays treatment that is already indicated. Supplementation alone does not reduce refracture risk, and about one in five such women fractures again within twelve months. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Osteoporosis Management)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Osteoporosis Management

options.text: Weekly oral alendronate 70 mg with calcium and vitamin D supplementation
options.rationale: Oral alendronate is the usual first choice after a minimal trauma vertebral fracture, but it is not recommended once the estimated glomerular filtration rate falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m2 because renal clearance of bisphosphonate falls with it. Her filtration rate has been stable at 28 for two years, so this is a fixed contraindication rather than a transient one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Bone and Metabolism)

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma vertebral fracture in a woman of this age is a treatment trigger in its own right and does not need bone densitometry confirmation before therapy starts. The decision then turns entirely on renal function, because the bisphosphonates are renally cleared and carry hard filtration rate floors. Oral bisphosphonates stop at 30 mL/min/1.73m2 and zoledronic acid at 35, both of which her stable rate of 28 falls below. Denosumab has no renal clearance pathway and is the preferred antiresorptive in this window, provided calcium and vitamin D are replete before the first dose.
key_points: A minimal trauma vertebral fracture establishes osteoporosis without needing a bone density result first
Oral bisphosphonates are not recommended below an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 30 mL/min/1.73m2
Zoledronic acid has a higher renal floor than the oral agents, not a lower one
Denosumab is cleared by the reticuloendothelial system and needs no renal dose adjustment
Correct vitamin D deficiency and confirm normal corrected calcium before the first denosumab dose
explanation.pearls: Check corrected calcium and 25-hydroxyvitamin D within the fortnight before every denosumab injection when the estimated glomerular filtration rate is under 30, because symptomatic hypocalcaemia in this group typically appears seven to fourteen days after the dose. Never allow a denosumab dose to lapse beyond seven months without transitioning to a bisphosphonate: rebound vertebral fractures cluster in the nine to eighteen month window after a missed injection.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners: Osteoporosis Management

subtopic_detail: glucocorticoid replacement adjustment in a patient on long term steroid replacement who presents with vomiting and cannot keep tablets down
stem:
You are the emergency department registrar. A 41-year-old man with a ten year history of primary adrenal insufficiency arrives with eighteen hours of vomiting and watery stools after a family barbecue. He took his morning hydrocortisone but vomited within twenty minutes and has kept nothing down since, including his afternoon dose and his fludrocortisone.

He is alert and answering fully, with dry mucous membranes and a capillary refill of three seconds. His pulse rate is 108 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg lying and 78/50 mmHg on standing, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent on room air and temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius. Bedside glucose is 4.1 mmol/L. Sodium is 129 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2) and creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), up from a baseline of 76. He carries an emergency card and an ampoule of hydrocortisone he has not used.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108 per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg lying and 78/50 mmHg standing, respiratory rate 18 per minute, SpO2 98 per cent room air, temperature 37.2 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and orientated, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill three seconds, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 4.1 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give 100 mg hydrocortisone intravenously now and restrict fluids given the sodium of 129 mmol/L
options.rationale: The steroid half of this is right, but the hyponatraemia here is hypovolaemic and driven by cortisol deficiency, so fluid restriction is exactly the wrong lever and would deepen the shock. The near pair is the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, where restriction is correct because the patient is euvolaemic, not orthostatic. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Corticosteroids)

options.text: Give 100 mg hydrocortisone intravenously now and start intravenous sodium chloride 0.9 per cent
options.rationale: Vomiting that prevents absorption of replacement steroid, with a postural drop, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and a rising creatinine, is an adrenal crisis and is treated on clinical grounds without waiting for confirmatory results. Parenteral hydrocortisone plus isotonic saline is the standard first action, and at stress doses the glucocorticoid provides enough mineralocorticoid effect that fludrocortisone is not needed acutely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give a double dose of oral hydrocortisone now and observe him for four hours before deciding
options.rationale: Doubling the oral dose is the correct sick day rule only while the patient is still absorbing tablets, and he has vomited every dose for eighteen hours. Once vomiting breaks the oral route, the rule explicitly switches to the parenteral one. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous fluids and antiemetics now and take a random cortisol before any steroid
options.rationale: A random cortisol has no role in a patient with established adrenal insufficiency on replacement, and holding steroid to obtain one risks cardiovascular collapse during the delay. Diagnostic sampling belongs to the undiagnosed patient, where the sample can still be drawn at the same time as the first dose is given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give calcium gluconate and an insulin dextrose infusion now for the potassium of 5.4 mmol/L
options.rationale: A potassium of 5.4 mmol/L without electrocardiographic change is mild, and here it is a marker of mineralocorticoid deficiency rather than a threat in itself. Treating the number distracts from the cause, and it corrects on its own once volume and glucocorticoid are restored. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: An established adrenal insufficiency patient who cannot retain oral steroid is in crisis until proven otherwise, and the postural drop with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and an acute creatinine rise confirms it. The management is parenteral hydrocortisone and isotonic saline together, given immediately and on clinical suspicion alone. Stress dose hydrocortisone saturates the mineralocorticoid receptor, so fludrocortisone can be safely omitted until oral intake resumes. The mild hyperkalaemia and the hyponatraemia are consequences, not separate problems, and both resolve with the primary treatment.
key_points: Vomiting that defeats oral absorption converts the sick day rule from doubling tablets to parenteral hydrocortisone
Treat adrenal crisis clinically and never delay steroid to obtain a cortisol level in an already diagnosed patient
Isotonic saline, not fluid restriction, is the correct response to hypovolaemic hyponatraemia in crisis
Fludrocortisone is unnecessary while hydrocortisone is being given at stress doses
Mild hyperkalaemia without electrocardiographic change needs no specific therapy in this setting
explanation.pearls: The triad that should trigger parenteral hydrocortisone before any result returns is a known adrenal insufficiency patient, a postural systolic drop of more than 20 mmHg, and any barrier to swallowing. Every patient on replacement should leave hospital with a 100 mg hydrocortisone ampoule, a written plan to double oral dosing for 48 to 72 hours with fever above 38 degrees, and instruction to inject at home and call an ambulance the moment vomiting starts.

subtopic_detail: interpreting pleural fluid biochemistry when the serum protein is low enough to make the absolute fluid protein misleading
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 69-year-old man admitted with four weeks of increasing breathlessness. He has alcohol related cirrhosis and has had two previous admissions for ascites, and he stopped drinking eight months ago. He has smoked twenty cigarettes daily for forty years.

A chest radiograph shows a moderate right pleural effusion, and you perform a diagnostic aspiration. The pleural fluid protein is 28 g/L and pleural lactate dehydrogenase is 176 units/L. His serum protein is 48 g/L (60-80), serum albumin 24 g/L (35-50) and serum lactate dehydrogenase is 310 units/L (120-250). Pleural fluid appearance is straw coloured, pleural glucose is 5.2 mmol/L, and the pleural fluid cell count shows a lymphocyte predominance. There is no fever and the white cell count is within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Stony dull percussion note and reduced breath sounds at the right base, moderate ascites, no peripheral stigmata of malignancy
data_table.Pleural fluid: Protein 28 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase 176 units/L, glucose 5.2 mmol/L, lymphocyte predominant, straw coloured
data_table.Serum: Protein 48 g/L (60-80), albumin 24 g/L (35-50), lactate dehydrogenase 310 units/L (120-250)

lead_in: How should you classify this effusion and what follows from it?

options.text: Indeterminate, because the glucose is 5.2 mmol/L, so repeat the aspiration in seventy two hours
options.rationale: Pleural glucose separates complicated parapneumonic and rheumatoid effusions from other exudates and plays no part in the transudate to exudate decision, so a normal value cannot make the classification indeterminate. Repeating the tap adds a procedure without adding information. (Source: British Thoracic Society: Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society: Pleural Disease Guideline

options.text: Exudative, because the fluid protein exceeds 30 g/L, so arrange pleural biopsy
options.rationale: The fluid protein is 28 g/L, which does not cross the absolute 30 g/L line, and that line is unreliable whenever serum protein is abnormal. Reaching for biopsy before the fluid has been classified correctly inverts the order of the workup. (Source: British Thoracic Society: Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society: Pleural Disease Guideline

options.text: Exudative, because the fluid to serum protein ratio exceeds 0.5, so investigate for malignancy
options.rationale: Light's criteria classify as exudative if any one is met, and the fluid to serum protein ratio of 0.58 crosses the 0.5 threshold even though the absolute fluid protein does not reach 30 g/L. Hypoproteinaemia from cirrhosis is precisely the setting where the absolute value misclassifies, and a lymphocytic exudate in a heavy smoker warrants cytology and computed tomography. (Source: British Thoracic Society: Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society: Pleural Disease Guideline

options.text: Transudative, because the fluid to serum lactate dehydrogenase ratio is below 0.6, so treat the ascites
options.rationale: Light's criteria are met if any single criterion is satisfied, so a lactate dehydrogenase ratio below threshold does not overturn a protein ratio that is above it. The near pair is hepatic hydrothorax, which is genuinely transudative and would satisfy none of the three criteria. (Source: British Thoracic Society: Pleural Disease Guideline)
source_refs: British Thoracic Society: Pleural Disease Guideline

options.text: Transudative, because the serum albumin is 24 g/L, so start diuretics and repeat the radiograph
options.rationale: A low serum albumin explains why an effusion forms but does not classify the fluid, and using it to override a positive Light's criterion is the specific error this presentation is built around. Diuresis without classification risks missing a treatable pleural malignancy for months. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Light's criteria classify an effusion as exudative when any one of three thresholds is crossed, and here the fluid to serum protein ratio of 0.58 crosses the 0.5 line. The absolute fluid protein of 28 g/L sits just under the traditional 30 g/L cut-off, which is exactly how hypoproteinaemic patients get misclassified as transudative. Cirrhosis lowers serum protein and so compresses the absolute value while leaving the ratio intact, making the ratio the trustworthy signal in this patient. A lymphocyte predominant exudate in a long term smoker then directs the workup toward malignancy and tuberculosis rather than toward diuresis.
key_points: Any one positive Light's criterion makes the effusion exudative; the others do not veto it
Fluid to serum protein ratio above 0.5 is criterion one, fluid to serum lactate dehydrogenase above 0.6 is criterion two
The absolute fluid protein of 30 g/L misclassifies when serum protein is low, as in cirrhosis or nephrotic syndrome
Pleural glucose addresses complicated parapneumonic and rheumatoid effusions, not the transudate to exudate split
A lymphocytic exudate in a smoker warrants cytology and contrast computed tomography of the chest
explanation.pearls: When a patient on diuretics or with cirrhosis sits within 5 g/L of an exudative threshold, compute the serum to pleural albumin gradient: a gradient above 12 g/L reclassifies the fluid as transudative despite a positive Light's criterion. Send at least 50 mL for cytology on the first diagnostic tap, since sensitivity for malignant effusion rises from roughly 60 per cent on one sample to about 75 per cent when a second specimen is taken on a different day.

sources.label: British Thoracic Society: Pleural Disease Guideline

subtopic_detail: fitness to hold a commercial vehicle licence in a driver with severe sleep apnoea who reports falling asleep at the wheel
stem:
You are the general physician seeing a 52-year-old man referred by his general practitioner. He drives a semi-trailer on the interstate route and holds a commercial licence. His wife reports loud snoring with witnessed pauses, and he tells you that three weeks ago he crossed the rumble strip after nodding off on a straight stretch near Dubbo, and that he now stops for coffee every ninety minutes to stay awake.

His body mass index is 38 kg/m2, neck circumference 46 cm, and his Epworth Sleepiness Scale score is 17 out of 24. A laboratory polysomnogram performed last week shows an apnoea hypopnoea index of 48 events per hour with oxygen desaturation to 78 per cent. His thyroid function and haemoglobin are within normal limits, and he takes no sedating medication. He tells you he cannot afford to stop driving and asks you to keep this between the two of you.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 38 kg/m2, neck circumference 46 cm, Mallampati class 4, no retrognathia
data_table.Investigations: Polysomnography: apnoea hypopnoea index 48 per hour, minimum SpO2 78 per cent; thyroid function and haemoglobin within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Arrange bariatric surgery referral and defer any driving decision until the weight has fallen
options.rationale: Weight reduction is a legitimate long term treatment and surgery may well be appropriate, but the benefit accrues over many months and leaves the immediate crash risk untouched. Deferring the licensing decision for that period is the part that fails. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Position Statement on Driving)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Position Statement on Driving

options.text: Respect his request for confidentiality and review him in the clinic again in three months
options.rationale: Confidentiality does not extend to withholding advice about a risk to the public, and a three month gap leaves him driving a heavy vehicle with an apnoea hypopnoea index of 48. If he continues to drive against advice, the treating doctor may report to the licensing authority under state provisions. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Prescribe modafinil for residual sleepiness and permit continued driving under regular review
options.rationale: Wake promoting agents are reserved for sleepiness that persists after airway pressure therapy is fully established, not as a first line for untreated disease. The near pair is treated apnoea with residual daytime somnolence, where modafinil is reasonable and the airway pressure is already optimised. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Position Statement on Driving)
source_refs: Australasian Sleep Association: Position Statement on Driving

options.text: Start continuous positive airway pressure and advise him not to drive commercially until treated
options.rationale: The Austroads standard is that a driver with severe obstructive sleep apnoea and a recent episode of falling asleep at the wheel is not fit to hold a commercial licence until effective treatment is established and adherence is documented. Starting therapy and giving clear written advice to stop commercial driving is the doctor's action, and the driver then has a legal duty to notify the licensing authority himself. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

options.text: Start continuous positive airway pressure and allow driving with a two hourly rest break schedule
options.rationale: Scheduled breaks and caffeine are compensations a sleepy driver invents and are not an accepted substitute for treatment under the commercial standard. He is already using this strategy and it did not prevent the near miss on the highway. (Source: Austroads: Assessing Fitness to Drive)

explanation.summary: An apnoea hypopnoea index of 48 with an Epworth score of 17 and a witnessed sleep episode at the wheel places this driver clearly outside the commercial fitness standard. Australian practice is that the treating doctor advises against commercial driving until therapy is established and adherence is objectively documented, and the driver carries the legal obligation to notify the licensing authority. Doctors may report directly where a patient continues to drive against advice, so the request for confidentiality does not bind you. Airway pressure therapy is the treatment that actually shortens the interval to safe driving, typically within weeks rather than the months weight loss requires.
key_points: Severe obstructive sleep apnoea plus a sleep episode at the wheel fails the Austroads commercial standard
The driver must notify the licensing authority; the doctor must advise and document that advice
State provisions permit a doctor to report a driver who continues against advice
Continuous positive airway pressure with documented adherence is the route back to a conditional licence
Wake promoting drugs treat residual sleepiness after therapy, not untreated disease
explanation.pearls: For a commercial licence, plan on documenting at least four hours of continuous positive airway pressure use per night on at least 70 per cent of nights, from device download rather than self-report, before supporting a conditional licence. An Epworth score above 15 combined with any reported sleep episode while driving should prompt the same advice even before polysomnography returns, because the crash risk does not wait for the sleep study.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Position Statement on Driving

subtopic_detail: reversal strategy for a supratherapeutic warfarin level accompanied by intracranial bleeding rather than isolated laboratory derangement
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the emergency department resuscitation bay. A 74-year-old woman on warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve was found on her bathroom floor by her son about an hour ago. She had struck her head on the vanity, and she now opens her eyes to voice, is confused in speech and localises to pain.

Her pulse rate is 58 per minute, blood pressure 178/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent on room air and temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. A non-contrast computed tomography of the head performed ten minutes ago shows a 12 mm right subdural collection with 4 mm of midline shift. Her international normalised ratio is 5.8, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-400) and creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90). She last took warfarin yesterday evening and the neurosurgical team has been called.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 58 per minute, blood pressure 178/94 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 per minute, SpO2 97 per cent room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Glasgow Coma Scale 12, pupils equal and reactive, no limb weakness, boggy right parietal scalp haematoma
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 5.8, haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-155), platelets 210 x10^9/L (150-400), creatinine 88 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Imaging: Non-contrast head computed tomography: 12 mm right subdural collection with 4 mm midline shift

lead_in: What is the most appropriate reversal strategy?

options.text: Prothrombin complex concentrate alone, withholding vitamin K given her mechanical mitral valve
options.rationale: The concern about compromising future anticoagulation is real but is not a reason to withhold vitamin K when the bleed is intracranial, because the concentrate's factors are consumed within hours and the international normalised ratio rebounds. The valve is managed afterwards with early reintroduction of heparin once the neurosurgical team judges it safe. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Warfarin Reversal Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Warfarin Reversal Guidelines

options.text: Fresh frozen plasma 15 mL/kg with intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg given together now
options.rationale: Plasma is second line in Australia because the volume needed to correct an international normalised ratio of 5.8 takes far longer to thaw and infuse and risks circulatory overload in a woman of this age. It is reserved for when prothrombin complex concentrate is unavailable. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Warfarin Reversal Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Warfarin Reversal Guidelines

options.text: Intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg alone with a repeat international normalised ratio in six hours
options.rationale: Vitamin K requires hepatic synthesis of new factors and takes six to twelve hours for meaningful correction, which is far too slow when a subdural collection is already shifting the midline. It is the right sole agent for a raised international normalised ratio with no bleeding, which is the near pair here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Withhold warfarin and give tranexamic acid 1 g intravenously with a repeat scan in six hours
options.rationale: Antifibrinolytic therapy does nothing about the missing vitamin K dependent factors that are the actual defect, so the coagulopathy persists whatever the fibrin clot is doing. Simply withholding the next dose leaves an international normalised ratio of 5.8 uncorrected for days. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Prothrombin complex concentrate with intravenous vitamin K 5 to 10 mg given together now
options.rationale: Warfarin associated intracranial haemorrhage requires immediate and durable reversal, which means prothrombin complex concentrate for the instant correction plus intravenous vitamin K to sustain it once the concentrate wears off at around six hours. Giving either alone leaves a predictable window of rebound anticoagulation while the bleed is still expanding. (Source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Warfarin Reversal Guidelines)
source_refs: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Warfarin Reversal Guidelines

explanation.summary: Warfarin associated intracranial haemorrhage is the most time critical reversal scenario in general medicine and demands correction within minutes rather than hours. Prothrombin complex concentrate replaces factors II, VII, IX and X directly and normalises the international normalised ratio almost immediately, but its effect is short lived. Intravenous vitamin K must be given alongside it so that endogenous factor synthesis resumes before the concentrate is consumed, otherwise the coagulopathy returns while the haematoma is still evolving. The mechanical valve is not a reason to soften reversal; it is managed by reintroducing anticoagulation early once the neurosurgical team agrees.
key_points: Prothrombin complex concentrate and intravenous vitamin K are given together, never sequentially, in major bleeding
The concentrate corrects in minutes but its factors are consumed within roughly six hours
Vitamin K alone takes six to twelve hours and is appropriate only when there is no bleeding
Fresh frozen plasma is second line in Australia because of volume and thawing delay
A mechanical valve does not justify partial reversal during intracranial haemorrhage
explanation.pearls: Anticipate the rebound: an international normalised ratio checked at 30 minutes after prothrombin complex concentrate looks reassuring and the one checked at six hours climbs again unless vitamin K was co-administered, so recheck at both time points. For a mechanical mitral valve, discuss restarting therapeutic heparin with neurosurgery at around 48 to 72 hours, because mitral prostheses carry a higher thrombotic risk than aortic ones during the anticoagulation gap.

sources.label: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood: Warfarin Reversal Guidelines

subtopic_detail: selecting an anticoagulant for a first venous thrombosis occurring during chemotherapy for an upper gastrointestinal tumour
stem:
You are the medical registrar on the oncology ward. A 63-year-old woman receiving her third cycle of chemotherapy for a locally advanced gastric adenocarcinoma reports three days of left calf swelling and aching. A compression ultrasound confirms thrombus extending from the popliteal into the superficial femoral vein, with no involvement above the common femoral vein.

She has no chest pain or breathlessness, and her observations are within normal limits. Her platelet count is 96 x10^9/L (150-400), haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45-90) and liver function tests are within normal limits. She has had two episodes of vomiting in the four days since her last cycle and describes intermittent epigastric discomfort, and an endoscopy six weeks ago showed a friable ulcerated tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction. She takes no antiplatelet agent.

data_table.Examination: Left calf 4 cm greater in circumference than the right, mild pitting oedema to mid-calf, no chest signs
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 96 x10^9/L (150-400), haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), creatinine 71 micromol/L (45-90), liver function within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Compression ultrasound: thrombus in left popliteal and superficial femoral veins, common femoral vein patent

lead_in: Which anticoagulation regimen would you start?

options.text: Therapeutic weight adjusted low molecular weight heparin given once daily by subcutaneous injection
options.rationale: Low molecular weight heparin remains the preferred agent for cancer associated thrombosis when the tumour is an unresected luminal gastrointestinal lesion, because the direct oral anticoagulants carry a higher rate of major gastrointestinal bleeding in exactly that setting. Her friable gastro-oesophageal junction tumour and recent vomiting make that the dominant consideration. (Source: eviQ: Cancer Associated Thrombosis)

options.text: Therapeutic oral rivaroxaban using the standard loading schedule then the maintenance dose
options.rationale: Rivaroxaban is a reasonable choice for many cancer associated thromboses and is more convenient, but the trials that established it showed excess major bleeding concentrated in patients with intact luminal gastrointestinal malignancy. A friable ulcerated tumour at the gastro-oesophageal junction is that exclusion in the flesh. (Source: eviQ: Cancer Associated Thrombosis)

options.text: Therapeutic oral warfarin bridged with low molecular weight heparin until the target range is reached
options.rationale: Warfarin performs poorly in active malignancy because vomiting, variable oral intake, antibiotics and chemotherapy destabilise the international normalised ratio, and recurrent thrombosis rates are higher than with heparin. It remains an option only when heparin and the direct agents are both unsuitable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Prophylactic dose low molecular weight heparin given the platelet count of 96 x10^9/L
options.rationale: A platelet count of 96 x10^9/L is well above the threshold at which dose reduction is considered, which is generally below 50 x10^9/L, so there is no basis for under-treating an established proximal thrombus. Prophylactic dosing for an existing clot invites propagation. (Source: eviQ: Cancer Associated Thrombosis)

options.text: Retrievable inferior vena cava filter insertion with anticoagulation deferred until platelets recover
options.rationale: Filters are reserved for patients in whom anticoagulation is genuinely contraindicated, and thrombocytopenia at this level is not such a contraindication. Inserting one here adds a device related thrombosis risk while leaving the original clot untreated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Cancer associated thrombosis is now treated with either low molecular weight heparin or a direct oral anticoagulant in most patients, so the exam point is knowing which tumours push the choice back toward heparin. Unresected luminal gastrointestinal malignancy, particularly gastro-oesophageal, is the principal exception because direct oral agents produced significantly more major gastrointestinal bleeding in the randomised trials. Her friable ulcerated junctional tumour and recent vomiting sit squarely in that exception. A platelet count of 96 x10^9/L is not low enough to modify the dose, and a filter has no role while anticoagulation remains safe.
key_points: Low molecular weight heparin is preferred for thrombosis with unresected luminal gastrointestinal cancer
Direct oral anticoagulants increase major gastrointestinal bleeding in gastro-oesophageal and gastric primaries
Warfarin underperforms in active malignancy because of erratic absorption and drug interactions
Dose modification for thrombocytopenia is generally considered below 50 x10^9/L, not at 96
Inferior vena cava filters are for genuine contraindications to anticoagulation, not for convenience
explanation.pearls: Anticoagulate for at least six months and continue while the cancer is active or treatment ongoing, reassessing at each cycle rather than stopping at an arbitrary date. When the platelet count falls between 25 and 50 x10^9/L on chemotherapy, halve the therapeutic heparin dose rather than stopping, and withhold entirely below 25 x10^9/L while transfusion support is arranged.

subtopic_detail: interpreting a positive interferon gamma release assay before starting tumour necrosis factor inhibitor therapy in an asymptomatic patient
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar in a combined clinic with rheumatology. A 44-year-old man who moved from Vietnam eleven years ago has rheumatoid arthritis that has failed methotrexate and leflunomide, and the plan is to start adalimumab. He has no cough, no fever, no night sweats and no weight loss, and he has gained 3 kg over the past year.

His pre-treatment screening shows a positive interferon gamma release assay. A chest radiograph is reported as showing no parenchymal abnormality, no cavitation and no apical scarring. He received bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination as an infant. Three induced sputum specimens collected for completeness are negative on acid fast smear and remain negative on culture at six weeks. His liver function tests and full blood count are within normal limits, and his alcohol intake is two standard drinks weekly.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrical small joint synovitis of the hands, chest clear on auscultation, no lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Interferon gamma release assay positive, three sputum acid fast smears negative, cultures negative at six weeks, liver function and full blood count within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph: no parenchymal abnormality, no cavitation, no apical scarring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management before adalimumab is started?

options.text: Proceed with adalimumab now and monitor symptoms with a chest radiograph every six months
options.rationale: Surveillance without prophylaxis accepts a reactivation risk that tumour necrosis factor blockade multiplies several fold, and reactivation under this class is disproportionately extrapulmonary and disseminated. Radiographic monitoring will not detect that pattern early. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Treat for latent infection with isoniazid and pyridoxine for nine months, starting adalimumab after four weeks
options.rationale: A positive interferon gamma release assay with no symptoms, a normal chest radiograph and negative cultures defines latent infection, and tumour necrosis factor inhibition carries a substantial reactivation risk that must be pre-empted. Australian practice is to begin latent treatment and allow the biologic to start after about four weeks of established therapy rather than waiting for the full course. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Treat for active disease with four drug therapy for six months, starting adalimumab after completion
options.rationale: Active disease requires symptoms, radiographic change or microbiological confirmation, and he has none of the three with cultures negative at six weeks. Full four drug therapy exposes him to unnecessary hepatotoxicity and delays effective arthritis control by half a year. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Attribute the assay result to prior bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination and proceed directly to adalimumab
options.rationale: Interferon gamma release assays use antigens absent from the vaccine strain, so vaccination does not cause a false positive, which is the specific advantage these assays hold over the tuberculin skin test. The near pair is a positive tuberculin skin test, where vaccine history genuinely confounds interpretation. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Latent Tuberculosis Infection

options.text: Repeat the assay in three months and defer any decision about adalimumab until that result returns
options.rationale: Repeating a positive assay in a person from a high incidence country adds nothing but a three month delay, since the pre-test probability makes a true positive far more likely than laboratory variation. Serial testing is used for conversion surveillance in occupational settings, not to second guess a single positive before immunosuppression. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Latent Tuberculosis Infection)
source_refs: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Latent Tuberculosis Infection

explanation.summary: The combination of a positive interferon gamma release assay, absent symptoms, a clear chest radiograph and negative cultures is the definition of latent tuberculosis infection. Tumour necrosis factor inhibitors substantially raise the risk of reactivation and skew it toward extrapulmonary and disseminated disease, so latent treatment is mandatory before the biologic begins. Isoniazid with pyridoxine for nine months is the standard Australian regimen, and the biologic may start after roughly four weeks of it rather than after completion. Bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination is irrelevant to the interpretation because the assay antigens are absent from the vaccine strain.
key_points: Latent infection is a positive immunological test with no symptoms, normal imaging and no microbiological growth
Interferon gamma release assays are unaffected by prior bacille Calmette-Guerin vaccination
Isoniazid with pyridoxine for nine months is the standard Australian latent regimen
Biologic therapy may begin about four weeks into latent treatment, not after completion
Reactivation under tumour necrosis factor blockade is often extrapulmonary and missed by chest radiography
explanation.pearls: Add pyridoxine 25 mg daily with isoniazid in anyone with diabetes, renal impairment, alcohol use or pregnancy, since peripheral neuropathy is the complication that stops patients completing the course. Check alanine aminotransferase at baseline and monthly, and stop isoniazid if it rises above five times the upper limit without symptoms or above three times with anorexia, nausea or right upper quadrant pain.

sources.label: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee: Latent Tuberculosis Infection

subtopic_detail: recognising when a rapidly progressive lower limb soft tissue infection requires theatre rather than escalation of intravenous antibiotics
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes admitted eight hours ago with a red, swollen left lower leg after a scratch from a rose bush. He was started on intravenous flucloxacillin on admission and the marked border has advanced about 8 cm up the calf since then.

He is asking repeatedly for more analgesia and has now had 20 mg of oxycodone with little effect, which the nursing staff say is out of proportion to what they can see. His pulse rate is 124 per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air and temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius. The skin over the anterior calf is dusky with two tense blisters that were not present on admission, and the calf feels woody to palpation. White cell count is 24.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 164 micromol/L (60-110), sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), lactate 4.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2) and creatine kinase 1840 units/L (40-200).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 per minute, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 per minute, SpO2 96 per cent room air, temperature 38.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dusky anterior calf with two tense blisters, woody induration, pain far exceeding visible findings, pedal pulses present
data_table.Investigations: White cells 24.1 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 164 micromol/L (60-110), sodium 129 mmol/L (135-145), lactate 4.2 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), creatine kinase 1840 units/L (40-200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Escalate to intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin tazobactam and review the leg in the morning
options.rationale: Broadening cover is part of the answer but is worthless alone, because the necrotic fascial plane is avascular and antibiotic does not reach it. The near pair is severe cellulitis, which does respond to antimicrobial escalation and does not show bullae, crepitus or woody induration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Measure compartment pressures at the bedside and elevate the limb pending the result
options.rationale: Compartment syndrome is the near pair for severe pain with a tense limb, but it follows trauma, reperfusion or a fracture rather than a spreading erythematous infection with fever and bullae. Pressure measurement delays the operation that both conditions would in any case require. (Source: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine: Sepsis Resources)
source_refs: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine: Sepsis Resources

options.text: Call the surgical team for immediate operative exploration while broadening antibiotics and resuscitating
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin with new bullae, woody induration and rapid progression despite appropriate antibiotics are the bedside hallmarks of necrotising soft tissue infection, and survival depends on the interval to debridement. Antibiotics and fluids are given in parallel with the call to theatre, never instead of it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the leg to confirm fascial involvement before surgery
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance is sensitive for fascial oedema but takes time this patient does not have, and a normal study does not exclude the diagnosis when the bedside picture is this strong. Imaging is for the equivocal case, not the one that is already declaring itself. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Calculate the laboratory risk indicator score and reassess the limb in two hours after fluids
options.rationale: The laboratory risk indicator was designed to raise suspicion in early ambiguous cellulitis, and it has a false negative rate high enough that it must never be used to delay theatre. Using a score to buy two hours is the specific anti-pattern here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a clinical diagnosis made at the bedside and confirmed in theatre, not in the radiology department. Pain disproportionate to the visible findings, rapid advance of the margin despite appropriate antibiotics, dusky skin with new bullae and woody induration together carry enough weight to mandate surgical exploration immediately. Physiological derangement with hypotension, a lactate of 4.2 mmol/L, hyponatraemia and a raised creatine kinase supports deep tissue necrosis rather than dermal infection. Antibiotic broadening and resuscitation happen alongside the surgical call, because only debridement removes the avascular necrotic plane.
key_points: Pain out of proportion plus advancing margins despite antibiotics mandates surgical exploration
New tense bullae, dusky skin and woody induration are late but decisive bedside signs
Imaging and scoring systems must never delay theatre when suspicion is high
Antibiotics cannot reach an avascular necrotic fascial plane
Hyponatraemia with a raised creatine kinase points to deep tissue necrosis rather than cellulitis
explanation.pearls: Mark the erythema border with a pen and time it: advance of more than 2 cm per hour despite intravenous antibiotics is a surgical trigger on its own, regardless of how well the patient looks. Add clindamycin to broad spectrum cover while awaiting theatre, because it suppresses streptococcal exotoxin production in a way that beta lactams alone do not.

sources.label: Australasian College for Emergency Medicine: Sepsis Resources

subtopic_detail: choice and pace of parenteral blood pressure lowering when very high pressure is accompanied by acute pulmonary oedema
stem:
You are the medical registrar in the emergency department resuscitation bay. A 66-year-old woman presents with two hours of severe breathlessness that woke her from sleep and forced her to sit upright at the window. She has never been admitted before and takes amlodipine, which she admits she stopped about six weeks ago when the packet ran out.

Her pulse rate is 112 per minute, blood pressure 226/128 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 per minute, SpO2 86 per cent on room air and temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius. She is using accessory muscles and has widespread inspiratory crackles to both mid zones with a third heart sound. Her chest radiograph shows bilateral perihilar alveolar opacification with upper lobe diversion. Troponin is mildly raised at 42 nanograms/L (<14) with no dynamic change on the repeat, the electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy and no ST elevation, and creatinine is 104 micromol/L (45-90).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 112 per minute, blood pressure 226/128 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 per minute, SpO2 86 per cent room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Sitting forward, accessory muscle use, bilateral inspiratory crackles to mid zones, third heart sound, no leg oedema
data_table.Investigations: Troponin 42 nanograms/L (<14) without dynamic change, creatinine 104 micromol/L (45-90), electrocardiogram sinus tachycardia with left ventricular hypertrophy
data_table.Imaging: Chest radiograph: bilateral perihilar alveolar opacification with upper lobe venous diversion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment of her blood pressure?

options.text: Oral captopril 25 mg with observation and repeat blood pressure measurement after thirty minutes
options.rationale: An oral agent cannot be titrated or withdrawn once absorbed, and its onset is too slow for a patient desaturating at 86 per cent on room air. Oral therapy belongs to hypertensive urgency without organ dysfunction, which is the near pair. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Intravenous labetalol boluses aiming to return the blood pressure toward normal within the hour
options.rationale: Beta blockade is preferred in aortic dissection but is relatively contraindicated in acute decompensated heart failure because the negative inotropy worsens pulmonary congestion. Driving the pressure to normal within an hour also overshoots the recommended reduction for most hypertensive emergencies. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council: Acute Cardiogenic Pulmonary Oedema)
source_refs: Australian Resuscitation Council: Acute Cardiogenic Pulmonary Oedema

options.text: Intravenous morphine 5 mg with oxygen and restarting her usual amlodipine at the original dose
options.rationale: Opioid is no longer recommended in acute pulmonary oedema because it depresses respiration and is associated with worse outcomes, and amlodipine takes hours to act. Neither addresses the immediate afterload problem. (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council: Acute Cardiogenic Pulmonary Oedema)
source_refs: Australian Resuscitation Council: Acute Cardiogenic Pulmonary Oedema

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion titrated with non-invasive ventilation and oxygen support
options.rationale: Acute pulmonary oedema with severe hypertension is driven by afterload and redistribution rather than by volume overload, so a titratable nitrate that drops preload and afterload within minutes is the correct lever alongside positive pressure ventilation. Unlike the other agents here it can be adjusted or stopped within minutes if the pressure falls too far. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Intravenous frusemide 80 mg as the sole agent with oxygen by non-rebreather mask alone
options.rationale: Loop diuretic has a role but is secondary here because this woman is not fluid overloaded, and the initial response to frusemide is transient venodilation rather than diuresis. Relying on it alone leaves the afterload that is actually causing the oedema untouched. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Sympathetic crashing pulmonary oedema presents with very high blood pressure, sudden onset and clear lungs on the way in, and it is a redistribution problem rather than a fluid excess problem. The treatment that changes the trajectory is aggressive afterload and preload reduction with a titratable nitrate, combined with positive pressure ventilation to recruit alveoli and reduce work of breathing. Loop diuretic has a supporting role and opioid is now discouraged because of respiratory depression and worse outcomes. Beta blockade is avoided in decompensated heart failure despite its usefulness in other hypertensive emergencies.
key_points: Severe hypertension with acute pulmonary oedema is an afterload problem, not primarily a volume problem
Titratable intravenous nitrate plus non-invasive ventilation is the combination that reverses the physiology
Loop diuretic is adjunctive; many of these patients are euvolaemic or dry
Beta blockade worsens decompensated heart failure and is reserved for dissection
Opioids are no longer recommended in acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema
explanation.pearls: Aim to drop the mean arterial pressure by no more than about 25 per cent in the first hour in most hypertensive emergencies, with the deliberate exceptions of aortic dissection, where the systolic target is under 120 mmHg within twenty minutes, and thrombolysis eligibility, where it is under 185/110 mmHg. A mildly raised troponin without dynamic change in this setting reflects demand ischaemia from wall stress and does not by itself mandate the acute coronary pathway.

sources.label: Australian Resuscitation Council: Acute Cardiogenic Pulmonary Oedema

subtopic_detail: preparing a patient for aldosterone to renin ratio testing when their current antihypertensives interfere with the result
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar in the hypertension clinic. A 46-year-old woman has had blood pressure above 160/100 mmHg for three years despite perindopril, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide taken together at maximal tolerated doses, and home readings confirm the clinic values. She has had two episodes of muscle cramps and her potassium has twice been recorded at 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2) without any potassium losing illness.

Her sodium is 143 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90) and bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22-32). Renal artery imaging performed last year was reported as normal, plasma metanephrines were within normal limits, and an overnight dexamethasone suppression test was normal. She has no family history of early stroke and takes no liquorice, no non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and no oral contraceptive. You plan to measure the aldosterone to renin ratio.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 168/104 mmHg, other vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No cushingoid features, no abdominal bruit, no radiofemoral delay
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2) on two occasions, sodium 143 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22-32), creatinine 74 micromol/L (45-90)
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide at maximal tolerated doses

lead_in: How should you prepare her for the test?

options.text: Replace potassium, continue all current agents and interpret the ratio against drug adjusted ranges
options.rationale: Amlodipine has a modest effect and could be continued, but a thiazide and an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor together push the ratio down strongly enough that no adjusted range rescues the interpretation. Correcting potassium alone leaves the dominant interference in place. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

options.text: Start spironolactone for the hypokalaemia and measure the ratio once the potassium has normalised
options.rationale: Mineralocorticoid receptor blockade is the single most powerful confounder of this test and must be withheld for at least six weeks beforehand, so starting it destroys the investigation you are planning. It is the correct treatment once the diagnosis and subtype are settled. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

options.text: Proceed to adrenal vein sampling first since the biochemical picture already indicates the diagnosis
options.rationale: Adrenal vein sampling is a subtype study performed after screening and confirmatory testing establish the diagnosis, not a substitute for them. The near pair is a confirmed case with a unilateral nodule on imaging, where sampling determines whether adrenalectomy will cure. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

options.text: Collect a twenty four hour urinary aldosterone instead and continue her current three agents unchanged
options.rationale: Urinary aldosterone excretion is used as a confirmatory test under salt loading, not as the screening test, and it suffers from the same drug interference as the plasma ratio. Substituting one interfered measurement for another does not solve the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Replace potassium, stop the thiazide for four weeks and substitute verapamil or prazosin for control
options.rationale: Thiazides raise renin and so lower the ratio, generating false negatives, and hypokalaemia itself suppresses aldosterone secretion, so both must be corrected before sampling. Slow release verapamil, prazosin and hydralazine have minimal effect on the ratio and are the substitutions used to keep the pressure controlled during the washout. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism

explanation.summary: Resistant hypertension on three agents with unprovoked hypokalaemia and a high normal sodium is a strong indication to screen for primary aldosteronism. The aldosterone to renin ratio is exquisitely sensitive to medication, and the two changes that must happen before sampling are correcting the potassium and withdrawing the drugs that distort renin most. Thiazides and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists raise renin and generate false negatives, while beta blockers suppress renin and generate false positives. Verapamil, prazosin and hydralazine are the interim agents that leave the ratio interpretable while keeping the patient safe during washout.
key_points: Screen for primary aldosteronism in resistant hypertension, unprovoked hypokalaemia or an adrenal incidentaloma
Hypokalaemia suppresses aldosterone and must be corrected before the ratio is measured
Thiazides and mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists cause false negatives by raising renin
Beta blockers cause false positives by suppressing renin
Adrenal vein sampling is a subtype study and follows confirmatory testing, never precedes it
explanation.pearls: Withhold mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists for six weeks and thiazides for four weeks before sampling, and take the sample mid-morning after the patient has been upright for at least two hours and seated for five to fifteen minutes. Roughly half of people with primary aldosteronism have a normal potassium, so never let normokalaemia talk you out of screening resistant hypertension.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Primary Aldosteronism
